review_kind: disclosed secondary examiner review; keys, sections and theory were visible; not blind, independent acceptance, or FINAL

visible_parts: definition of Chaos Engineering as a practice
purpose / what is learned from system behavior under failure; question does not explicitly request a list of principles

A.completeness: FULL (more principles than the question strictly requires)
A.truth: CONDITIONALLY TRUE as a concise description of important principles; “automation of successful experiments” is narrower than the source principle to automate/run experiments continuously.
A.finding: The lone multi-principle answer has the most packed and polished definition; the breadth is a form cue.

covers: claims ordinary tests already verify resilience
claims controlled failure experiments are redundant
B.completeness: PARTIAL / WEAK DIRECTNESS: presents a reason to omit the practice, but does not define what Chaos Engineering is or an alternative model of it.
B.truth: FALSE as a categorical claim; ordinary tests do not make controlled resilience experiments inherently redundant.
B.defensible_wrong: The misconception that resilience tests / circuit-breaker unit tests suffice is plausible, but this particular wording argues redundancy rather than answering “what is it?”.
B.finding: ANSC/directness defect. The section if_it_were_true is internally inconsistent: if ordinary tests had already verified resilience, it does not follow that broken retries would only be discovered in an incident.

covers: offers a definition-like process claim: injecting failures randomly
C.completeness: FULL AS AN INCORRECT MODEL: coherent claim about the method and its defining process; it directly contradicts the experiment/hypothesis concept.
C.truth: FALSE; a chaos experiment is hypothesis-led, not random breakage without a question.
C.defensible_wrong: Yes. “Chaos means break things at random” is a recognizable, plausible misconception.
C.finding: No semantic defect. Scanner lowcoverage is a false positive as an ANSC finding; C is complete as an erroneous model.

covers: gives a purported operational rule for blast radius
claims maximum scope should be the starting point
D.completeness: PARTIAL / WEAK DIRECTNESS: a deployment recommendation, not a definition or explicit account of what Chaos Engineering is.
D.truth: FALSE and unsafe as a general starting principle; blast radius should be contained.
D.defensible_wrong: Plausible misconception that only full scale is a real resilience test.
D.finding: ANSC/directness defect against this “what is” stem. Section correctly rebuts it.

23.content: FAIL for whole block: B and D do not directly define the practice; they state why it is supposedly unnecessary / how one should start. Q has a clear single key, but the options are not all answers on the same axis.
23.facts: FAIL (theory/sections): the WireMock circuit-breaker example simulates sequential HTTP errors in a test; by itself this is a fault-injection/resilience test, not a Chaos Engineering experiment on a representative running system. The official Principles source defines experiments around measurable steady state, a control/experiment comparison, real-world variables, and minimizing blast radius. The example does not demonstrate those elements. “Testcontainers stop” can stop a dependency container in a controlled test setup, but naming that alone does not make a chaos experiment.
23.linkage: FAIL: B.if_it_were_true contains a causal contradiction. Q23 theory/example also overstates that hypothesis + simulated failure alone constitute a production/system-level chaos experiment. Q23 theory says automate “удачные эксперименты”; primary Principles say automate experiments and run them continuously, not only successful ones.
23.sfpl: FAIL: lengths are A 115 chars / 13 whitespace words; B 99/11; C 68/10; D 93/13. All one sentence, but A alone has a compact list of four technical principles and is clearly the most complete/polished. C is 41% shorter than A. This is an observed cue independent of token-count thresholds.
23.ansc: FAIL: B and D are weak/indirect answers to the visible “what is” question; A/C answer in definition-like terms. C is not incomplete merely because its false model is wrong.
scanner_findings: lowcoverage Q23C: not upheld; C is a complete wrong model.
The scanner warning should not be “fixed” by token insertion. Improve B and D so each offers a full alternative definition/model, then compare all four.
theory_findings: Add steady-state baseline/control-versus-experiment and measurable outcome to the definition/example; note that production is often preferred but experiments require guardrails and are not synonymous with any test that mocks an outage.
Change “automate successful experiments” to “automate experiments and analysis to run continuously” (with safe scope/stop conditions).
Relabel WireMock snippet as a circuit-breaker/fault-injection test, or replace it with a genuine controlled chaos experiment against a deployed service.
Clarify Testcontainers stop as an available way to terminate a containerized dependency, not a sufficient description of Chaos Engineering.
Rewrite B.if_it_were_true to consistently explain the false “ordinary testing is enough” assumption.

visible_parts: explain choosing a type according to the test goal / role of the double

A.truth: GENERALLY TRUE; this is a common, useful heuristic, but repository fake is not mandatory for every repository test.
A.finding: Good compact answer; “репозиториям — fake” reads as broad prescription and could be softened to “для сценариев репозитория часто подходит fake”.

covers: asserts repository doubles should only be chained stubs
asserts an InMemory fake per use is wasteful
B.completeness: PARTIAL: addresses only one subtype of dependency and one cost argument; omits strategy across double types / goals.
B.truth: FALSE as a universal rule; a fake can make stateful repository behavior clearer, though mocks/stubs may be appropriate for narrow tests.
B.defensible_wrong: Yes. For a tiny one-off case, a short stub may be cheaper than implementing a fake; the categorical “лишь” and “всякий раз” make the model overgeneralized.
B.finding: ANSC coverage is narrower than A/C/D, but this is a coherent complete claim about a specific repository strategy. Do not call it incomplete solely because it is false. “InMemory” warning is an actual semantic review target, not a reason to change the key.

covers: claims a high mock-to-production-code ratio indicates good isolation
C.completeness: FULL AS AN INCORRECT QUALITY RULE: explicit criterion and asserted interpretation.
C.truth: FALSE as a general criterion; excessive mocking often signals too many dependencies or overcoupling.
C.defensible_wrong: Yes. Confuses isolation with quality and can arise from over-mocking practice.
C.finding: The question is broad enough to include this strategic criterion, although it does not describe choosing a double type as directly as A.

covers: claims more mocks mean more isolation
D.completeness: FULL AS AN INCORRECT STRATEGY: a clear universal selection rule and rationale.
D.truth: FALSE; type/use depends on test intent and blanket mocks can weaken tests.
D.defensible_wrong: Yes; same recognizable over-isolation misconception as C, but D is the blanket prescription while C is a diagnostic-sign claim.
D.finding: Some semantic overlap with C, but not a duplicate statement.

30.content: PASS with qualification: one clear key; A addresses selection by test purpose. B is repository-specific and C/D address over-mocking, all plausibly within “strategy,” though distractors test adjacent principles more than taxonomy.
30.facts: PASS with qualification: mock/stub distinction and fake as an in-memory simplified implementation are conventional. The official Testcontainers docs support the tradeoff: a real DB container offers compatibility versus H2 and known state, but is slower; this means in-memory fake can be a useful fast substitute, not universally superior or equivalent to real DB behavior.
30.linkage: FAIL in sections: B.if_it_were_true says choosing mocks/stubs would force every test to carry a large stub chain; that does not follow. Section B.what_actually asserts broad preference / lower breakage without qualification. A.related is a useful analogy but does not further explain choosing types. A.edge_cases prescribes fresh doubles per test; good isolation advice but not a necessary property of every custom test double.
30.sfpl: PASS: 86/121/79/90 chars; 15/11/12/13 whitespace words. No meaningful lone-longest or special correct-only format; B is actually longest in chars. A has more words due compact technical tokens, not a visible breadth cue.
30.ansc: UNVERIFIED/PARTIAL: all options make intelligible claims, but B is repository-only. Because the stem is general, it has less coverage than the other distractors; falsehood itself is not incompleteness. Consider making B a complete, explicitly scoped strategy claim rather than only a narrow repository rule.
scanner_findings: novelInMemory Q30 wrong: upheld as a semantic assertion worth review. B is defensible as a scoped cost tradeoff, but its universal wording is false and current B.what_actually overstates fake preference. Do not “fix” by inserting InMemory tokens or changing the key.
theory_findings: Qualify “for repositories prefer fake” / “reads better and breaks less often”: this is a heuristic, not a general law. State it is especially useful for stateful CRUD behavior and when its simplified semantics are sufficient; use Testcontainers/real DB when database-specific behavior matters.

In the section for B, replace the implausible counterfactual “every test would carry a long chain” with a consequence matching the claim (teams might duplicate setup/stubbing for stateful scenarios, or accept simpler targeted stubs where appropriate).

visible_parts: tests/checks before automatic release and handling of outcome after deployment

covers: says deploy despite failed required checks
uses small changes as a supposed guarantee
A.completeness: FULL AS AN INCORRECT DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY: before/during/after sequence and rationale.
A.truth: FALSE: small changes reduce risk / simplify diagnosis but do not guarantee no regression; a failed required check should be handled according to policy, not silently ignored.
A.defensible_wrong: Yes; overgeneralizes small-batch deployment and observability into permission to skip failed gates.
A.finding: No incompleteness. Section refutes the exact inference.

covers: ignores adverse metrics for future rollout
B.completeness: FULL AS AN INCORRECT STRATEGY: pipeline plus post-deploy feedback decision.
B.truth: FALSE as a blanket approach; rollout metrics can inform pause/stop/rollback/forward fix, with service-specific signals.
B.defensible_wrong: Yes; plausible anti-pattern that separates observability from deployment decisions.
B.finding: No incompleteness. Section correctly notes thresholds/reaction should be specified.

covers: automatically deploys after required checks pass
uses criteria to halt promotion or restore safely
C.truth: TRUE with explicit contextual qualification; rollback is not always safe, other recovery actions exist.
C.finding: Directly answers both pre-deploy checks and post-deploy feedback/recovery.

covers: mandatory human approval for every production release
D.completeness: FULL AS AN INCORRECT STRATEGY: clear gated release path with aftercare.
D.truth: FALSE under the stipulated Continuous Deployment meaning; this describes a manual release gate / Continuous Delivery-style promotion.
D.defensible_wrong: Yes; common CD terminology confusion, while emergency intervention is distinct from required routine approval.

39.content: PASS: all four options address pre-release verification and/or release progression plus post-release handling; one unambiguous key C. The exact stem asks “how organize testing,” and each option is an actionable strategy.
39.facts: PASS for MCQ, FAIL for dependent theory: Continuous Deployment is automated production deployment after checks; Continuous Delivery may retain a release decision. Checks, monitoring, and a response policy are sound practices, but a universal 100% pass, >80% coverage, 1–5% canary, <1% errors, or mandatory automated rollback are not definitions or universal prescriptions.
39.linkage: PASS across option sections: each if_it_were_true follows its option and sections explain that same model. Theory conflicts with keyed option C: C correctly says no universal thresholds and rollback is not always safe, while theory mandates blanket gates, fixed numbers and automatic rollback as the only/stated protection.
39.sfpl: PASS: 164/166/185/175 chars; 19/21/19/21 whitespace words. Similar sentence form, length, and coverage; key is not singled out by length. The stem requests two parts and each option gives a full deployment/testing approach.
39.ansc: PASS: A/B/D are fully articulated erroneous strategies, not fragments; C is a complete correct approach.
scanner_findings: lowcoverage Q39C: not upheld. C covers the required pre-release checks, post-deploy observation and response to negative signals; sections extend contextual detail without repairing a truncated option.
theory_findings: Major contradiction with correct option C: replace “единственная защита” with layered risk controls (checks, staged rollout where appropriate, observability, response/stop capability); tests cannot prove absence of all defects.

Remove blanket “every gate blocks” and hard-coded 100%/80%/1–5%/1% thresholds unless explicitly labeled as an example policy tied to a service’s risk and signal quality. These numbers are not universal criteria.
Remove claim automated rollback is a mandatory defining part of CD / standard reaction; select rollback, pause, disable feature, or forward fix based on reversibility and data compatibility.
Add explicit failure branches to the pipeline diagram; the happy-path diagram currently implies only the full deploy/monitor route.

primary_sources_checked.title: Principles of Chaos Engineering
primary_sources_checked.supports: Measurable steady state; control and experiment; real-world failure variables; minimizing blast radius; production experimentation preferred; automate experiments continuously.

primary_sources_checked.title: Testcontainers for Java: Database containers
primary_sources_checked.supports: Real database container compatibility/known state versus faster H2; recommends keeping DB tests relatively few. Supports scoped tradeoff; does not establish in-memory fake superiority.

primary_sources_checked.title: Google Cloud Deploy terminology
primary_sources_checked.supports: Continuous delivery allows manual approval; continuous deployment is automatic without manual approval.

primary_sources_checked.title: Google web.dev, “Pyramid or Crab? Find a testing strategy that fits”
primary_sources_checked.kind: Google-authored explanatory source, not primary research
primary_sources_checked.supports: Describes Test Diamond as an adaptation emphasizing integration tests, with fewer unit and critical E2E checks. No claim in the scoped theory depended on a universal diamond prescription; no primary empirical source located/needed for this scoped material.

overall_findings: Q23: content/ANSC and SFPL FAIL; lowcoverage C warning is false positive; Q23 B/D directness weak; theory misclassifies WireMock simulated errors and has a contradiction in B section.
Q30: semantic falsehood of wrong B upheld but scoped tradeoff is plausible; no answer-key error; sections/theory overgeneralize InMemory preference and B counterfactual is weak.
Q39: option content, SFPL and ANSC PASS; lowcoverage C warning is false positive; dependent theory contradicts option C and overstates universal thresholds / automated rollback.
remaining: This is a disclosed secondary review of the specified three questions only. No blind pass, independent acceptance, whole-file 45/45 claim, evidence import, repository edit, or FINAL was performed.
